records.text: Owens said Pierre Falcone's partner Arkadi Gaydamak was also involved in Angolagate, which she described as global trafficking at the highest levels of government.
records.speaker: Candace Owens

appearances.snippet: And obviously yesterday we spoke about this Pierre (Pierre Falcone) in Scottsdale and I had mentioned that he had a partner, Pierre Falcone had a partner named Arkadi Gaydamak. ... Didn't expect that to be relevant to anything, but they were both involved in Angola Gate, which was global trafficking at the highest levels of government.

verification.notes: Reliable contemporaneous reporting confirms that Arkadi Gaydamak and Pierre Falcone were the two principal defendants associated with the Angolagate arms-sales and corruption case. That supports Owens' statement that both were involved. Her description of the matter as global trafficking at the highest levels of government is broader and more rhetorical than the established record, which concerned arms sales to Angola, influence peddling, corruption, and senior French political figures. The core association is confirmed but the characterization is overstated.

records.text: Owens cited a Global Witness report saying Arkady Gaydamak funneled billions of dollars in arms and oil-backed loans to Angola's government for oil contracts, and that Gaydamak and Pierre Falcone transferred about $463 million in arms using Jean-Christophe Mitterrand's access to the Angolan government.
records.speaker: Candace Owens

appearances.snippet: According to All the Presidents' Men, a March 25th report on Angolagate by Global Witness, Gaydamak funneled billions, billions of dollars in arms and oil-backed loans to Angola's government in return for lucrative oil contracts. With Western oil companies. Falcone and Gaydamak, relying on the special access that Mitterrand had to the Angolan government, managed to transfer some $463 million in arms to Angola.

verification.notes: Global Witness's report page confirms the title, subject, and arms/oil focus of All the Presidents' Men. A contemporaneous article summarizing that report uses the same details Owens cited: Gaydamak allegedly funneled billions in arms and oil-backed loans for oil contracts, while Falcone and Gaydamak used Jean-Christophe Mitterrand's access to transfer about $463 million in arms. This verifies the citation as a faithful report of what the cited material alleged, not independent proof of every allegation in the NGO report.

records.text: Seven anonymous email tipsters told Owens they believed Arkadi Gaydamak was living near Nashville as Jonathan Schmidt and working for Root Brands, with the reported move occurring sometime in June 2025.
records.speaker: Anonymous Source #3 (Ep t4U7NjnUEgc)

appearances.snippet: I was shocked when a flutter of emails came in from people saying that they believed Gaydamak was living in Nashville. ... that he moved here sometime in June, okay? And when I say a flurry of emails that came in, there were seven people, mostly men, who were certain that that man, aged now, is working in Nashville using the name Jonathan Schmidt. ... They are certain at the very least that he is from Israel and that he is working for a company known as Root Brands under the guise of being a technology officer.

verification.notes: The transcript is explicit that this came from seven email correspondents and that Owens would correct it if wrong. Searches found only derivative reposts of Owens broadcast, not identity records, corporate filings, employment confirmation, or a statement from Gaydamak, Schmidt, or Root Brands. The proposition now preserves both the anonymous sourcing and belief qualifier.

records.text: Owens said Arkadi Gaydamak failed to appear for his court hearing and was sentenced in absentia for weapons trafficking.
records.speaker: Candace Owens

appearances.snippet: But this Arkadi Gaydamak didn't show up for his court hearing. and he just was sentenced in absence for trafficking weapons, et cetera, et cetera.

verification.notes: Contemporaneous reporting confirms Gaydamak did not appear and was sentenced in absentia in October 2009 to six years for his role in arms trafficking to Angola. The historical statement is accurate as to the trial judgment. Important later context: in April 2011 the Paris appeals court acquitted him of illegal arms trading and influence peddling while retaining convictions on other counts, so the 2009 arms-trafficking conviction was not the final appellate disposition.

records.text: Owens cited an article as stating that Arkadi Gaydamak had been a French intelligence agent.
records.speaker: Candace Owens

appearances.snippet: He was also a factually, and you can see in this article, a French intelligence agent. Okay?

verification.notes: Transcript context confirms Owens pointed to an article and called Gaydamak a French intelligence agent. Current reporting establishes that former French officials, including Charles Pasqua and a former DST deputy director, publicly described Gaydamak as an agent or source for French counterintelligence, so an article making the cited claim exists. However, contemporaneous French reporting also documented sharply divergent intelligence-service assessments and described some claims about him as unconfirmed. The citation is real, but the underlying status is contested rather than established as an uncontested fact.
